title: Air Algérie 2208

agencies.name: Agenzia Nazionale per la Sicurezza del Volo

summary: Air Algérie Flight 2208, a cargo Hercules at 24,000 feet, began descending for unknown reasons while autopilot was engaged. The autopilot failed and disengaged; moments later both directional and longitudinal control were lost. The aircraft descended steeply at 45-50 degrees and impacted terrain near Piacenza 73 seconds after autopilot failure light illuminated, killing all three crew members. Investigation found no mechanical failure of aircraft systems.
probable_cause: The accident resulted from autopilot malfunction causing loss of aircraft control during descent (p. 14-20). The investigation found no mechanical failure of the airframe or primary flight control systems (p. 14-20).

factors.evidence: Autopilot was engaged during cruise at 24,000 feet and disengaged 12 seconds after the autopilot failure light illuminated (p. 14-16).
Both directional and longitudinal control were lost immediately after autopilot disengaged (p. 14-16, 20).
Aircraft lost control moments after autopilot failure light came on; crashed 73 seconds after the light illuminated with aircraft in 45-50 degree descent (p. 16-20).
Aircraft descended from 24,000 feet in steep 45-50 degree descent angle at impact speed approximately 460 knots (p. 20).

events.text: Aircraft at 24,000 feet over Italian territory with autopilot engaged when autopilot failure light illuminated (p. 14).
AP FAIL warning activated on aircraft (p. 14).
Autopilot disengaged 12 seconds after failure light illumination; directional and longitudinal control immediately lost (p. 14-16).
Aircraft began steep descent at 45-50 degrees; crew reported engine power loss to Milan ATC before losing radio contact at 13,500 feet (p. 16-17).
Aircraft descended through 10,000 feet in continuous steep descent (p. 17-18).
Aircraft approached terrain at high descent rate (p. 18-19).
Aircraft altitude continued descent at high rate toward impact (p. 19).
Aircraft impacted terrain at Besurica between Milan and Parma at steep 45-50 degree angle with estimated impact speed 460 knots, destroying fuselage and killing all three crew members (p. 20).

notes: Italian ANSV report; sections read: Flight recorders section (p. 14-20), investigation findings
